questions.prompt: What does the Linux filesystem's standard layout (like `/etc` for config, `/var/log` for logs) provide?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: A predictable structure that lets you find a service's configuration or logs on any Linux machine without guessing

The standardized directory layout is exactly what makes navigating an unfamiliar Linux server predictable rather than a guessing game.
keyPoints: The standardized directory layout is exactly what makes navigating an unfamiliar Linux server predictable rather than a guessing game.

questions.prompt: What is a shell script, fundamentally?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: A sequence of commands saved to a file and run as a single repeatable unit, with support for variables, conditionals, and loops

A shell script is just ordinary interactive commands captured into a reusable, automatable sequence — not a fundamentally different kind of artifact.
keyPoints: A shell script is just ordinary interactive commands captured into a reusable, automatable sequence — not a fundamentally different kind of artifact.

questions.prompt: What is the relationship between a container image and a running container?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: An image is a read-only template; a container is a running instance created from that image, and many containers can run from the same image

The image-to-container relationship is like a class-to-object relationship: one template, potentially many independent running instances.
keyPoints: The image-to-container relationship is like a class-to-object relationship: one template, potentially many independent running instances.

questions.prompt: According to the lesson, why does externalizing configuration into a ConfigMap matter?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: The same container image can run in different environments with different configuration, without rebuilding the image

The lesson's core point about ConfigMaps is that separating config from the image lets one image run in staging vs. production with different settings, with no rebuild required.
keyPoints: The lesson's core point about ConfigMaps is that separating config from the image lets one image run in staging vs.
production with different settings, with no rebuild required.

questions.prompt: Per the "🔀 The problem" section, why does merging get harder the longer branches stay isolated?
questions.referenceAnswer: The lesson describes this as integration hell — divergence compounds over time, making later merges involve more conflicting assumptions and touched files than early, frequent ones would.
keyPoints: The lesson describes this as integration hell — divergence compounds over time, making later merges involve more conflicting assumptions and touched files than early, frequent ones would.

choices.text: Because Git has a hard technical limit on how old a branch can be before merging
Because more files get touched and more conflicting assumptions accumulate the longer changes diverge, making conflicts bigger and integration more expensive
Because CI pipelines automatically delete old branches
Because longer-lived branches use more disk space

questions.prompt: Per the "⚡ Fast feedback" section, what kinds of checks typically run on every single push?
questions.referenceAnswer: The lesson names unit tests, linting, and type checking specifically as the fast tier meant to run on every push for near-immediate feedback.
keyPoints: The lesson names unit tests, linting, and type checking specifically as the fast tier meant to run on every push for near-immediate feedback.

choices.text: Full end-to-end test suites and performance benchmarks
Unit tests, linting, and type checking — cheap, numerous checks that catch the large majority of simple mistakes quickly
Nightly security scans
Manual QA review

questions.prompt: Per the "🪣 Object storage" section, what access pattern is object storage built for?
questions.referenceAnswer: The lesson describes object storage as suited to whole-file, infrequent access at massive scale, prioritizing durability over low latency — the opposite profile from a database's active data files.
keyPoints: The lesson describes object storage as suited to whole-file, infrequent access at massive scale, prioritizing durability over low latency — the opposite profile from a database's active data files.

choices.text: Frequent small random reads/writes from a single instance
Large files read or written as whole objects, infrequently, prioritizing durability and scale over low latency
Shared filesystem semantics across many instances with POSIX file locking
Sub-millisecond latency for database transaction logs

questions.prompt: Per the "🔐 Beyond base64" section, what does production-grade secrets management add beyond a base64-encoded Secret object?
questions.referenceAnswer: The lesson lists these three specific additions — encryption at rest, access control, dedicated secrets managers — as what actually provides real protection beyond bare base64 encoding.
keyPoints: The lesson lists these three specific additions — encryption at rest, access control, dedicated secrets managers — as what actually provides real protection beyond bare base64 encoding.

choices.text: Nothing — base64 encoding is already sufficient protection
Encryption at rest, fine-grained access control, and often a dedicated secrets manager rather than relying solely on the orchestration platform's built-in Secret objects
Only a longer base64 string
A requirement that secrets be stored in plaintext for easier debugging

questions.prompt: GPU workloads remain pending in a cluster. What would you inspect first, and why?
questions.referenceAnswer: Inspect scheduling events and resource requests. Check available GPU capacity, node labels and device plugins. Verify quotas and placement constraints before adding nodes.
keyPoints: Inspect scheduling events and resource requests.
Check available GPU capacity, node labels and device plugins.
Verify quotas and placement constraints before adding nodes.

questions.prompt: How would you test that the change fixed this incident rather than hiding it?
questions.referenceAnswer: Keep a reproducible failing case for this incident. Verify quotas and placement constraints before adding nodes. Compare the same workload before and after the change; record both the target metric and regressions.
keyPoints: Verify quotas and placement constraints before adding nodes.
Compare the same workload before and after the change.
Check regressions as well as the target metric.

questions.prompt: The fix works in a small test but fails at production scale. What next?
questions.referenceAnswer: Inspect scheduling events and resource requests. Measure representative workloads and separate resource, data and configuration differences. Stage a rollout with a rollback condition and rerun the original failure case.
keyPoints: Inspect scheduling events and resource requests.
Measure a representative workload.
Stage rollout and define rollback criteria.
